escapeBrief:
A storm in the night brought the supply line down near dawn, and every electric dial in the house stopped at 6:30: the player is never told, but the bulbs hang dark, the apparatus is dead and they move by torchlight. Mid-ladder they get the power back, and the dials pick up from where they stopped, so from then on every one reads 7:00. A dozen clocks agreeing is the trap: they agree because they share one master clock and stopped together.

Two clocks are not on the electric system. The keeper's weight-driven regulator, behind a secret door that opens only once the power is back, never stopped: its pendulum swings and it reads 9:15. A wind-up mantel clock has run down at 11:40, its pendulum still; the duty roster shows whose job it was to wind it, and a note shows they left early for the weekend.

The way out is the back gate from the glasshouse range to the station lane, just past the far end of the big glasshouse: the caretaker has locked the house for the weekend and taken the key. The gate's time-lock runs on the same circuit as the dials. After a power cut the dials have to be advanced by the minutes they lost, and the gate opens when that advance is set. The answer is 135 (9:15 on the running regulator minus 7:00 on the dials), on a three-digit keypad. The gate takes minutes, not a time, so copying any clock face does nothing: the player has to see why the dials are wrong together. That is the boss rung's move: the power cut has an effect on one kind of clock and none on the other, and the answer is the size of the effect where it applies.
title: The Last Train
subtitle: Rothamsted Experimental Station, a foggy November morning in the late 1920s
story:
You have one job before the morning train to London: finish the report on the barley pot trial in the glasshouses and take it with you. Forty-eight pots, each given a watering (sparing, moderate or generous), a soil (clay or sand), and potash or none. The Director's draft says soil makes no difference and every pot should be watered generously. Work out how much of the difference in grain each treatment explains, and whether the draft holds.

A storm blew through in the night, and near dawn it brought the power line down. Every electric clock on the station stopped at the same moment. The caretaker has locked the house for the weekend and taken the key, so the only way out to the station lane is the back gate beyond the glasshouses, and its time lock runs on the same circuit as the clocks: it will not open until the clocks are set right. You do not know whether your train has already gone.

debrief.title: What you did
debrief.intro: This scenario was analysis of variance on a barley pot trial: forty-eight pots, each given a watering, a soil and potash or none. You measured how much of the variation in grain the watering explains on its own, ranked the three treatments by that share, then fitted watering and soil together and read the interaction row first. Soil explained almost nothing on its own, yet it decided which watering was best: on clay, moderate watering gave the most grain, although generous watering was best on average. Here is what you did.

done.title: The report is finished
done.body: Soil explains almost nothing on its own, yet it decides the watering: on clay, moderate watering gives the most grain, although generous watering wins on average. The Director's draft will need rewriting. Now get to the station.

escapeDone.title: Set right
escapeDone.body: The dials agreed with each other all morning, and they were wrong for the same reason: they stopped together when the line came down. You set them forward by the minutes they lost, the time lock on the gate clicks, and it swings open onto the lane and the fog. The station is a short walk away, and there is still time for the train.

plannedHotspots.title: Splitting the variation
plannedHotspots.body: In a paper written at this station, R. A. Fisher and W. A. Mackenzie grew a dozen potato varieties under several different manures and asked whether every variety answered the manures alike. To find out, they split the total sum of squares into parts: the manures, the varieties, the varieties' differing response to the manures, and the scatter between plots treated the same. Their verdict: the varieties responded alike. That table of parts is the analysis you are running today.
plannedHotspots.credit: R. A. Fisher and W. A. Mackenzie, "Studies in crop variation II," Journal of Agricultural Science
